title: AI Can Spot Pancreatic Cancer Up to 16 Months Before Doctors, Johns Hopkins Surgeon Says
excerpt: A Johns Hopkins researcher highlights advances in AI-powered cancer detection that could transform outcomes for one of the deadliest cancers, while a new vaccine shows promise in intercepting the disease.
body:
Key Takeaways

  • The PanTS dataset includes over 36,000 CT scans from 145 medical centers for cancer detection.
  • A Phase 1 vaccine trial showed no progression to tumors in vaccinated patients with precancerous cysts.
  • Early detection can increase pancreatic cancer's five-year survival rate from 13% to 44%.

  • AI models can identify signs of pancreatic cancer up to 16 months ahead of human radiologists, according to Johns Hopkins surgeon Dr. Peter A. Najjar
  • Johns Hopkins researchers, collaborating with NVIDIA, built PanTS — the largest open-source CT scan dataset for pancreatic cancer detection, with over 36,000 scans from 145 medical centers
  • A separate Johns Hopkins Phase 1 vaccine trial showed zero progression from precancerous cysts to tumors in vaccinated patients
  • Pancreatic cancer has an overall five-year survival rate of just 13%, but early detection can raise it to 44%

Artificial intelligence is closing in on one of medicine’s most elusive targets: catching pancreatic cancer before it turns lethal.

Dr. Peter A. Najjar, a surgeon and clinical innovation vice president at Johns Hopkins Health System, told Fox Business that AI models are now able to identify signs of pancreatic cancer up to 16 months ahead of human readers — a timeline that could mean the difference between a treatable diagnosis and a death sentence.

“Researchers were able to identify signs of pancreatic cancer up to 16 months ahead of human readers,” Najjar said. “Detection always allows us more treatment options.”

Why Early Detection Matters

Pancreatic cancer is the third-leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States, with 80% to 85% of cases diagnosed too late for effective treatment. According to the American Cancer Society, the overall five-year relative survival rate is just 13%. But when the cancer is detected before it spreads beyond the pancreas, that rate climbs to 44%.

The disease’s silent progression and the anatomical complexity of the pancreas make it exceptionally difficult for radiologists to catch early. It has claimed the lives of several high-profile figures, including Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, actor Patrick Swayze, and Jeopardy! host Alex Trebek.

![Johns Hopkins. The PanTS Dataset: AI at Scale At the research level, Johns Hopkins computer scientists have built the infrastructure needed to train AI models for population-scale screening.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/Hopkinsp.jpg)

The PanTS Dataset: AI at Scale

At the research level, Johns Hopkins computer scientists have built the infrastructure needed to train AI models for population-scale screening. In collaboration with NVIDIA and institutions worldwide, they created the Pancreatic Tumor Segmentation Dataset, or PanTS — the largest fully open-source CT scan dataset for pancreatic cancer detection.

The dataset contains over 36,000 3D CT scans from 145 medical centers, with expert-validated annotations of more than 993,000 anatomical structures. Each scan includes metadata on patient age, sex, diagnosis, and imaging protocols, enabling models that can work across diverse populations and imaging conditions.

“Although current AI isn’t yet ready for population-wide screening, if we use imaging biomarkers, clinical notes, and deep neural networks to select high-risk patients, we can transform a blunt screener into a precision detection tool.”

— Zongwei Zhou, Johns Hopkins Assistant Research Professor

The dataset was built using NVIDIA’s MONAI Label, an open-source AI framework for medical imaging, and was presented at the 39th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

A Vaccine for Cancer Interception

In a separate but related breakthrough, Johns Hopkins researchers reported promising results from a Phase 1 clinical trial of a pancreatic cancer vaccine targeting patients with precancerous cysts and lesions. At a 16.5-month median follow-up, none of the vaccinated participants had any progression to pancreatic tumors. Three patients had their cysts completely resolve, and another three saw their lesions regress.

“Overall, this study represents the first proof of concept for the use of vaccines for interception of pancreatic cancer in human patients,” said oncologist and study co-author Dr. Neeha Zaidi.

Beyond Detection: AI in Drug Discovery

Najjar noted that AI is also accelerating drug discovery for pancreatic cancer. Scientists are now able to test potential treatments using computer models before moving into laboratory testing, potentially compressing the years-long drug development pipeline.

Another Johns Hopkins innovation, the ARTEMIS-DELFI blood test, uses AI to detect DNA fragments shed by tumors circulating in a patient’s blood. Published in Science Advances, the technique could help clinicians quickly determine whether pancreatic cancer therapies are working — critical for a disease where every week of ineffective treatment narrows the window for alternatives.

While Dr. Najjar stressed that more real-world evidence is needed before AI’s full impact on cancer care can be measured, the convergence of early detection, immunization, and treatment monitoring marks a turning point for a disease long considered a near-automatic death sentence.
